articles.title_orig: Prediction: This Artificial Intelligence (AI) Memory Stock Will Go Parabolic on Oct. 30
articles.title_zh: Prediction: This Artificial Intelligence (AI) Memory Stock Will Go Parabolic on Oct. 30
articles.content_orig:
As technology companies race to build data centers, demand for the memory chips that make artificial intelligence (AI) computing possible has skyrocketed. One of the leading manufacturers of memory chips for AI hyperscalers is Micron Technology ( MU +2.77% ) .
So far this year, Micron stock has soared 225% -- making it the third-highest performer in the Nasdaq-100. Nevertheless, Micron's shares have experienced considerable volatility over the last couple of months and trade about 24% below their all-time high.
I think this disconnect is about to reverse. On Oct. 28 and 29, Alphabet ( GOOGL +1.19% ) ( GOOG +0.84% ) and Amazon ( AMZN +1.61% ) are scheduled to report quarterly earnings. While investors will undoubtedly focus on their respective AI-related capital expenditures (capex), I think another topic could emerge as a major discussion point: the global memory shortage. If my prediction is accurate, Micron could begin to rally just in time for Halloween.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 10/27/26
For most of the AI revolution, investors primarily associated infrastructure with graphics processing units (GPUs) designed by Nvidia and application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) designed by Broadcom . However, GPUs and custom silicon cannot operate efficiently without sufficient memory. Micron manufactures dynamic random access memory (DRAM) and high bandwidth memory (HBM), both of which are critical components of the AI chip stack.
Interestingly, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy already highlighted the growing importance of memory during the company's last earnings call. Jassy explained that Amazon planned to increase its 2026 capex budget to $220 billion -- up from its previous forecast of $200 billion -- specifically because of higher memory costs.
Meanwhile, Alphabet raised its 2026 capex forecast to $195 billion to $205 billion during its second-quarter earnings call. Management attributed the increase to accelerating infrastructure investments and capacity supply constraints. Although Alphabet did not explicitly identify memory as the culprit, its comments reinforce the underlying idea that demand for AI compute is insatiable.
As both companies prepare to report earnings this week, investors should pay close attention to any additional commentary surrounding memory availability, pricing, and infrastructure spending.
Image source: Getty Images.
Amazon and Alphabet aren't the only companies confronting the memory shortage. Earlier this month, Elon Musk took to X (formerly Twitter) to discuss the bottlenecks facing AI infrastructure build-outs. Musk specifically identified RAM supply as a constraint, supporting the idea that memory availability is becoming just as important as access to advanced processors.
This distinction matters because the AI infrastructure boom is moving beyond simply procuring as many GPUs as possible. AI models need memory to support training and inference. Training involves teaching AI to recognize patterns , while inference occurs when those models are deployed to perform an actual task rather than just answer a query. Both activities require substantial memory, particularly as applications become more complex across autonomous systems, robotics, and agentic AI.
A prolonged memory shortage could create favorable conditions for Micron. When demand for a product exceeds available supply, manufacturers can command higher prices . For Micron, this is already happening and translating into accelerating revenue growth, expanding profit margins, and earnings visibility.
MU Revenue (TTM) data by YCharts
One of the biggest headwinds dragging on Micron stock right now is skepticism about the semiconductor industry's boom-and-bust cycles and whether hyperscalers can maintain the pace of their infrastructure spending. I think Amazon's and Alphabet's upcoming earnings reports will help answer that question.
If leadership explicitly emphasizes the memory shortage, rising component prices, or the increasing demand for memory-intensive AI applications, investors may begin to view Micron's growth as more durable than anticipated.
My prediction is that earnings season will become a turning point for Micron stock. If the world's largest AI developers stress the industry's memory shortage, investors should recognize that Micron's opportunity extends well beyond this year. With shares still trading meaningfully below their all-time high, positive commentary could provide a much-needed catalyst for a new rally.

articles.title_zh: Dollar General sued by FTC and 20 states, accused of overcharging customers
articles.content_orig:
Piper Sandler managing director Jake Oubina discusses how household wealth is driving a consumer spending boom. The panel analyzes surging mortgage rates, multi-decade high Treasury yields and rising oil prices.
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 20 states filed a lawsuit on Monday against Dollar General over alleged deceptive pricing practices.
The FTC and states claimed that Dollar General, over a period of years, had repeatedly mislabeled prices, overcharged consumers and failed to correct the issue despite corporate knowledge of the problem. Dollar General has disputed those claims.
Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement that "Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last."
"The FTC's action underscores the agency's commitment to lowering costs for consumers by stopping deceptive pricing practices that harm Americans," Mufarrige added.
INSTACART AGREES TO $60M CONSUMER REFUNDS AFTER FTC ACCUSES COMPANY OF HIDDEN FEES AND FORCED SUBSCRIPTIONS
Dollar General was hit with a lawsuit by the FTC and 20 states over alleged deceptive pricing practices. (Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
The complaint said that thousands of Dollar General stores have taken advantage of vulnerable shoppers by extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges with insufficient safeguards to prevent the practice.
It added that the company has received tens of thousands of complaints from consumers across the country who said the company didn't honor the advertised price , which suggests there has been widespread consumer harm to shoppers around the country.
States that joined the FTC lawsuit include Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
FTC DECLARES JULY AS 'MADE IN THE USA' MONTH
Dollar General disputed the claims made in the FTC complaint and said the proposed settlement was excessive. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Dollar General disputed the claims made in the suit filed by the FTC and states, saying in a statement that "The lawsuit filed today by the Federal Trade Commission and several states suggests that we have abandoned our mission and willfully disregarded the affordability needs of our customers. Nothing could be further from the truth."
"Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store. As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer," Dollar General said.
The company's statement said that it was made aware of the FTC investigation in early February 2026 and that it "engaged cooperatively" with the FTC and made several company representatives available to provide sworn testimony on relatively short notice.
WANT TO CANCEL A SUBSCRIPTION? FTC FINALIZES RULE TO MAKE IT EASIER FOR CONSUMERS
Dollar General said that after the FTC concluded sworn testimony, it received a draft complaint along with a draft settlement which demanded a monetary amount that was "untethered to – and orders of magnitude larger than – any realistic assessment of amounts attributable to pricing discrepancies."
The company said that it worked in good faith with the FTC over the next four weeks and explained its issues with the agency's findings, then made a counteroffer for a monetary settlement before the agency filed suit.

articles.title_orig: Report: iPhone 18 Pro sales down 4% in the US, but China drives 3.1% global growth
articles.title_zh: Report: iPhone 18 Pro sales down 4% in the US, but China drives 3.1% global growth
articles.content_orig:
Counterpoint Research’s latest report offers a look at global iPhone 18 Pro sales during the first three weeks of availability. Here are the details.
In a report released today, Counterpoint Research says iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max sales in the US fell 4% during their first three weeks of availability compared to the first three weeks of iPhone 17 Pro series sales last year.
The report noted that Japan saw a whopping 27% drop in sales, with demand weakening “as exchange rates amplified the price increases.”
China, on the other hand, saw a 29% increase in sales, while other markets collectively recorded a more modest 3.1% increase.
The report doesn’t break down what that means in units, or millions of units, but it does offer some context on what drove these regional differences.
A regional breakdown shows that the global 3.1% growth was concentrated in specific markets. China posted the strongest growth, with sales rising 29% YoY. This was driven by better early supply compared with last year and by price increases on competing flagship models from Chinese Android OEMs. Excluding China’s contribution, the global sales growth rate would have been far weaker. The US and Japan experienced a YoY decline, affected by higher prices compared with their predecessors. In the US, consumers largely do not perceive meaningful improvements over the previous models in either features or design, while in Japan, demand has contracted as exchange rates amplified the price increases.
Today’s report also includes another interesting tidbit: According to Counterpoint, the iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for a slightly smaller share of Pro-series sales compared to last year’s iPhone 17 Pro series, which the firm attributed to higher prices and stronger demand for the smaller Pro model in emerging markets:
The iPhone 18 Pro Max accounted for 56% of sales within the iPhone 18 Pro series, a slight decrease from 57% last year. This can be attributed to the higher prices compared with last year, as well as the fact that the sales growth in emerging markets such as India and Southeast Asia skewed more toward the Pro models.
As to how, or whether, the iPhone Duo had any effect on these shifting numbers, the report didn’t address that directly, since the device launched after the three-week period covered by the data. However, Counterpoint Associate Director Sujeong Lim raised the possibility that it could affect Pro Max sales going forward:
“Whether China’s outperformance reflects durable demand or front-loaded buying will become clearer in the coming weeks. The recovery of US and Japanese volumes, and whether the iPhone Duo launching in Week 43 will generate incremental demand rather than cannibalising Pro Max, are the two most consequential near-term variables.”

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's worst nightmare may be lurking inside Anthropic's IPO filing
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's worst nightmare may be lurking inside Anthropic's IPO filing
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is hedging its bets by using multiple chips to handle its AI work — a strategy that could eventually erode Nvidia's dominance.
The AI lab says it manages compute "as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners" — with software that can direct its work to different chips depending on where they're most productive, according to Anthropic's S-1 filing , which came out Monday as the company prepares to go public.
Anthropic says it uses hardware from four chip families: Amazon Trainium, Google TPUs, Nvidia GPUs, and AMD GPUs.
That flexibility, which Anthropic said "took years and significant investment to build," could make major AI companies less dependent on Nvidia over time and give them more negotiating leverage, analysts said.
"The real exposure could be Nvidia's pricing power," said Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy, "because a customer that can shift work across four platforms negotiates very differently than one that can't."
Ashish Nadkarni, an analyst at IDC, added that a multichip approach also makes Anthropic less vulnerable to fluctuations in Nvidia's chip supply.
Although Anthropic's chip mix isn't new, the company is now pitching it as a core advantage to investors, Moorhead said.
The threat has its limits. Switching between chips is still difficult — especially when it comes to training AI models as opposed to running them, Moorhead said — and only the biggest AI companies have the resources to do it.
Anthropic also continues to spend billions on Nvidia compute , Moorhead said.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said that while other major companies like OpenAI likely take a multichip approach, it may not be worth the effort and investment for smaller players.
Brad Gastwirth, global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, said Anthropic's strategy doesn't represent a major near-term threat. Having more chip options doesn't erase Nvidia's advantages in performance, networking, and software, he said.
There's a broader risk for Nvidia if AI compute becomes more of a commodity.
Citadel CEO Ken Griffin has warned that if supply overtakes demand, it could drive down rental prices.
"GPUs, like airlines, have a very low marginal cost to run," he told Bloomberg last week. "The moment you have overcapacity, pricing goes into freefall."
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider.

articles.title_orig: Google begins certifying Registered App Stores for Android, but not in the US
articles.title_zh: Google begins certifying Registered App Stores for Android, but not in the US
articles.content_orig:
Running an app ecosystem has gotten a lot more complex for Google after its loss in the Epic Games antitrust case. While US users can access app stores in Google Play by court order, international users will use Google’s voluntary Registered App Stores program . Google has announced that stores wishing to be part of that program are now free to apply, and support will roll out to some Android devices later this year.
App stores accepted into the program will enjoy preferential treatment on the Android platform. Users of approved stores will be able to install apps with a single click, similar to the experience in the Play Store. These stores will also be allowed to update apps silently in the background like Google’s store does.
“In March, we announced the Registered App Stores program to give third-party app stores a more streamlined way to reach users while maintaining the safety and security of the Android ecosystem,” said a Google spokesperson. “Eligible app stores outside the US can now apply to register their stores ahead of the new simplified installation experience rolling out to users later this year.”
The Android Registered App Stores program was initially Google’s backup plan. After losing its appeal of Judge James Donato’s verdict, Google was faced with a number of remedies, like allowing third-party billing and sharing app catalogs with rival stores. The most dramatic shift was the court’s requirement that Google distribute third-party stores within Google Play.
Google and Epic, having patched things up following the trial, attempted to settle the case in a way that gave Google more control. Registered App Stores were intended as a replacement for hosting the stores in Google Play, provided they could adhere to a baseline level of trust and safety. Google intended to use this program in the US and internationally, but the companies withdrew the settlement when the court signaled it would not be approved.
Registered App Stores are still happening on Android, but they won’t be supported in the US—you can go to Google Play for alternative stores stateside, but so far, Aptoide remains the only one listed . Those operating Android app storefronts who want to be included in the international program can now review the program and begin the enrollment process.
Any store hoping to get approval will have to adhere to a number of requirements , including protecting intellectual property, removing illegal content, and publishing a privacy policy for both users and developers. Google also requires several ongoing security measures to ensure the stores do not give malware easier access to Android devices. As part of the application process, store operators must provide documentation for all these points (in English) and upload copies of all their apps.
It costs $10,000 per year to participate in the Android Registered App Stores program, and that fee must be paid before Google will review the application. Google says this fee covers the additional support necessary to run the program. There may also be additional review fees if Google detects a store has a problem with malware.
Google plans to roll out support in dozens of nations , which includes most of the world outside of the US and Europe. The program goes live on December 1, but it will only work on Android devices running the latest builds of Android 17. Google says support will start with Android 17 QPR2, which is expected to arrive on Pixel phones in the coming weeks. Google doesn’t even sell those in most of the supported regions, and the devices people do use in such places tend to have much slower updates. A substantial number of Android devices in supported countries may never even see an update compatible with the Registered App Stores program.

articles.title_orig: UPS CEO says delivery company will make more money on slightly fewer holiday deliveries
articles.title_zh: UPS CEO says delivery company will make more money on slightly fewer holiday deliveries
articles.content_orig:
United Parcel Service on Tuesday reported third-quarter results that beat Wall Street expectations and raised its full-year guidance.
The guidance raise comes after the company already upped its outlook last quarter . UPS now said it's projecting full-year consolidated revenue of approximately $92.6 billion, up from its previous expectations of $91.2 billion, as well as fourth-quarter revenue of $25.7 billion.
Shares of UPS rose slightly in morning trading.
Here's how the company performed in its third quarter, compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the quarter ended Sept. 30, UPS reported net income of $1.16 billion, or $1.37 per share, down slightly from net income of $1.31 billion, or $1.55, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time expenses, UPS reported earnings per share of $1.69. Revenue rose 6.7% to $22.9 billion.
In its domestic segment, the company said it saw a 4.5% increase in revenue, while its international segment had a 7.1% rise in revenue. Its supply chain solutions business saw an 18.2% revenue increase, which UPS said was primarily driven to growth in forwarding and logistics, including healthcare . On a call with analysts, CEO Carol Tomé said healthcare revenue exceeded $3 billion for the third consecutive quarter.
The company had previously said it expected its third-quarter domestic revenue to be flat and for domestic average daily volume to fall due to seasonal declines and the glide down with Amazon .
"We're driving more premium growth, improving revenue quality and mix, and creating greater operating leverage through a more efficient network," Tomé said on the call. "All of this is strengthening the underlying performance of our business."
UPS has been in the midst of a turnaround under Tomé's leadership, working to create a leaner business model and leveraging automation to position the company for growth.
As the company prepares for its peak holiday season, Tomé said the consumer remains resilient, and the growth in average daily volume between the third and fourth quarters will be consistent with last year. However, fourth-quarter domestic average daily volume is expected to fall due to the reduction with Amazon.
She added that nearly 70% of all packages will flow through an automated process this holiday season.

articles.title_orig: Why Anthropic's IPO contrasts the 'cult of Elon Musk' at SpaceX and Tesla
articles.title_zh: Why Anthropic's IPO contrasts the 'cult of Elon Musk' at SpaceX and Tesla
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
In the first mega IPO of 2026, SpaceX ( SPCX ) singled out one person in its prospectus as the shot caller: none other than the world's richest person, Elon Musk.
The next big IPO of the year — Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ), which could be the largest of all time — is run more by a committee of founders. That's a good thing given its mission and structures, according to veteran dealmaker Jim Neeson.
"I would say having seven founders working together can make it where it's not just like a cult of Elon Musk, right?" the Connor Group founding executive said on Sozzi Unleashed . "You actually have it where you have a consortium of people making decisions, which I actually think can be a good thing."
Neeson noted that Anthropic is a public benefit company with seven founders who collectively own 50.1%.
"You have a board that will be approved by sort of a trust fund. And then you also have a business where it's not just going to be about profits. It's also going to be sort of the social benefit piece that's built into their doctrine," he explained.
Anthropic's founders are CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and president, Daniela Amodei, as well as Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Chris Olah. The consortium left OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) to start Anthropic in January 2021.
The seven co-founders will be issued new Class F common stock as part of the IPO, giving them majority control of the company — something Neeson said investors will have to navigate.
"If you look at Meta, [and] you also look at Google, you had very strong founders," Neeson said. "A lot of times that is the venture capital case. I want founders that can make strong decisions and not be beholden to sort of quarterly type of trends."
"This is going to be a different type of structure out there, and it's going to be tested," he added. "We've never seen it, especially at this scale, especially at these growth rates. So I would say that's one thing analysts and investors are going to be looking very closely at."
The group looks to be managing the financials relatively well.
Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus showed. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.
On an adjusted basis, Anthropic posted $1.62 billion in operating income through the first six months of 2026 compared to a loss of $1.85 billion last year.
Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.
Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November. It plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

articles.title_orig: Oil Futures Fall as Market Holds Out Hope for Middle East Diplomacy
articles.title_zh: Oil Futures Fall as Market Holds Out Hope for Middle East Diplomacy
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices edged lower on Tuesday as the potential for a resolution in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran kept supply fears at bay, but Brent stayed close to six-month highs as attacks on Saudi Arabia lowered hopes of immediate stability in the region.
Brent crude futures were down 66 cents, or 0.57%, at $115.15 a barrel as of 0000 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude was down 44 cents, or 0.43%, at $101.32.
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday aimed at easing tensions in the Middle East. Saudi Arabia said the visit sought to establish open negotiating channels to "prevent the return of military escalation". The four countries agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation in peace and security, Iranian state media reported.
Hopes of resolution in the conflict erased some fears of supply disruption, lowering risks and pressuring oil prices.
However, losses were limited as scope for peace looked fragile, with renewed attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on key producer Saudi Arabia.
October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, according to data compiled by a Washington-based think tank that has tracked maritime security incidents worldwide since 2017.
The war has rippled across the Middle East, placing the Strait of Hormuz at the center of the turmoil. The narrow waterway carried around a fifth of the world's energy supplies before the conflict erupted in February.
Last week, Brent prices surged to more than $117 a barrel, the highest level since April, after a wave of Iranian attacks on tankers around the strait. Brent prices touched $117 on Monday as well.
Elsewhere, Russian refiners are raising diesel production in October after the government granted export quotas following the Kremlin's supply agreement with the US, two industry sources close to the matter said.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine war latest: Zelensky reveals details of 'Operation Veles'
articles.title_zh: Ukraine war latest: Zelensky reveals details of 'Operation Veles'
articles.content_orig:
Help us keep bringing the truth to light, even when Russia turns the lights out.
Key developments on Oct. 27:
Ukrainian forces " eliminated " more than 100 Russian soldiers and captured more than 30 others during an operation involving underground gas pipelines near Kupiansk in Kharkiv Oblast, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 27.
"The Russians had already tried to use underground gas pipelines to move through our positions and launch assault operations. Ukrainian warriors have successfully transformed this tactic, modernized it, and made it much more sophisticated and technologically advanced," Zelensky said.
The operation, code-named "Veles," involved an underground advance of more than 15 kilometers (9 miles), according to Zelensky .
The operation was carried out by the National Guard's 2nd Khartiia Corps alongside other Ukrainian units.
Zelensky said he had received reports on the operation's initial results and progress from Commander-in-Chief of Ukraine's Armed Forces Mykhailo Drapatyi, 2nd Khartiia Corps Commander Ihor Obolienskyi, and Deputy Head of the Presidential Office Pavlo Palisa.
The 2nd Khartiia Corps previously reported on Oct. 22 that Ukrainian troops had infiltrated Russian rear positions near Kupiansk through underground gas pipelines as part of Operation Veles .
The operation followed earlier Russian attempts to use the same tactic in the area. On Sept. 12, Ukrainian battlefield monitoring group DeepState reported that Russian troops had used a gas pipeline to cross the Oskil River and penetrate Ukrainian defenses near Kupiansk.
A localized ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has been "expanded… within Kherson (Oblast)," U.S. First Lady Melania Trump said in a post on social media on Oct. 27.
The ceasefire, which came into effect in the early hours of the morning, initially covered Oleshky and surrounding areas in Kherson Oblast and is meant to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and the delivery of humanitarian aid over the coming days.
Trump did not specify the extent of the expanded ceasefire but Tetiana Shelest, head of communications for Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, told reporters it now covered the entirety of Kherson Oblast.
According to a statement from Lubinets, the ceasefire was being "fully honored," with Ukraine and Russia adhering to the agreement as of 5:30 p.m. on Oct. 27.
"I hope that everything will continue in accordance with the agreed plan and that we will be able to help the civilians in Oleshky who are eagerly awaiting assistance," he added.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson , it has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, who prevent humanitarian aid from entering.
Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
Trump added that the timing was accelerated by two days to protect civilians and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid.
Earlier, Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, confirmed a "bilateral ceasefire" began in the embattled Oleshky, in a statement on Oct. 27.
The ceasefire will last until Nov. 1, David Arakhamia , the parliamentary leader of the president's Servant of the People party, said in a later post on social media. Lubinets added that the ceasefire will remain in effect until 10:59 p.m. Kyiv time on Nov. 1.
The agreements were reached in negotiations with Yana Lantratova, head of the Russian negotiating team.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a deadly attack overnight on Oct. 26-27, striking a university campus, a major bridge, an administrative building, and medical facilities.
Kyiv, a city of three million people, has been relentlessly assaulted by Russian ballistic missiles in recent months as Moscow exploits Ukraine's air defense shortage. While its battlefield offensive has slowed, Russia has chosen a strategy of mass aerial strikes against vulnerable civilians.
At least one person was killed, and 15 people have been injured in the latest Russian attack , Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Those injured in the attack include a paramedic, a medical technician, and a 20-year-old university student.
The mayor later reported a strike on the city's Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River, one of Kyiv's major traffic arteries. The bridge connects the city's eastern and western sides and is crucial for the daily commutes of hundreds of thousands of residents.
The bridge and metro infrastructure were damaged overnight, Klitschko said. Train service on the bridge has been temporarily suspended.
Ihor, who lives on the east bank of the Dnipro River but works on the west bank, said his commute now takes around two hours, including about half an hour spent walking across the Southern Bridge.
"We’ll have to walk like this every morning now. Taking a detour would take too long," Ihor, who declined to give his surname, told the Kyiv Independent.
Iryna was also crossing the bridge while it remained closed to traffic, but she was using an electric scooter to get across. Following the overnight attack on Oct. 27, this was her first time commuting to work this way.
"This is an alternative means of transport, but I don’t know how long the journey will take," Iryna, who also declined to give a surname, said, expressing hope that the bridge would be repaired soon.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that a university campus in the city was struck by Russia alongside Kyiv's well-known Kyoto park and residential buildings.
Education minister Andriy Butenko later said that the Russian attack damaged buildings and dormitories of the State University of Trade and Economics. He said there were no deaths among university students or employees.
"This is once again a terrorist country attacking educational institutions. A university, a scientific institution, a college, a school, or a kindergarten - the enemy directs its missiles at children, teachers, and scientists without any pity or humanity. There is no excuse for Moscow's cynical actions," Butenko added.
Ukrainian postal and courier company Nova Poshta has started its own private air defense force and shot down Russian attack drones targeting their facilities, Vyacheslav Klymov, co-owner of the Nova group of companies, revealed at the Kyiv International Economic Forum on Oct. 26.
"We are one of the few companies that has implemented this project. I don't want to disclose the numbers, but we have destroyed 'Shahed' drones, " Klimov said.
Nova Poshta is the largest private postal and courier company in Ukraine, operating over 15,817 branches across the country, and employing over 34,000 people. Its post offices and distribution centers have frequently come under Russian attack .
Despite the ongoing war, business is going well for Nova Poshta. The company quadrupled its net profit compared with last year, according to financial reports published on April 27.
Klimov also emphasised the importance of companies having their own private firefighting capabilities, rather than just waiting for the response of state authorities.
Nova Poshta employees frequently put out significant fires on their premises before the arrival of state emergency service firefighters, Klimov said.
"Now big businesses are looking for fire engines in Europe in order to create their own services. This is our property… who can forbid me from putting out a fire on my own territory?" he said.
Since late summer , Russia has been attacking Ukraine with jet-powered drones, adding to the now-familiar threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles. Between larger assaults, successive waves of jet-powered drones now arrive day and night.

articles.title_orig: American consumers are paying 8x more in fuel costs than the rest of the world, report finds
articles.title_zh: American consumers are paying 8x more in fuel costs than the rest of the world, report finds
articles.content_orig:
The Iran war continues to weigh on Americans’ wallets, and it’s costing them more in increased fuel costs than consumers in any other country in the world, new data finds. As President Donald Trump argues the cost of the war will be justified with economic prosperity, his administration may be pushing policies making the problem worse.
U.S. consumers have paid an average of $471 more in fuel prices since the beginning of the Iran war in February, according to a report published on Monday by Finland-based nonprofit research institute Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA). That’s nearly eight times greater than the average of about $60 in increased energy costs per person globally. As a country, the U.S. has spent $160 billion total on increased fuel costs since the beginning of the war, with China following at $54 billion, and Canada coming in third at $17 billion.
The Iran war has cost U.S. households about $2,000 , according to Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, a sum that includes both soaring prices at the gas pump as well as increased airfares and inflation as a result of increased transportation expenses and supply-chain shuffles over the last seven months of Middle East turmoil.
Trump has repeatedly tried to assuage Americans’ anxieties about increased costs associated with the war. At a rally in North Carolina in September, the president downplayed affordability concerns . He has argued the war is necessary to prevent Iran from attaining nuclear weapons, and that the U.S. is making a “ freaking fortune ” as a result of increased energy production.
“It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done,” Trump said last month of fuel costs, which have now topped $4.26 per gallon, up from $2.98 before the war. “Remember that.”
The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.
To be sure, the Iran war did not create the conditions under which American consumers in particular are paying higher energy costs. While global supply strains have increased fuel prices globally, the outsize impact on U.S. consumers is a result of an American economy and culture structured around oil.
“If you compare the U.S. with countries in Europe with similar levels of income, you can really see the effect of decades of lower prices for fuel and less emphasis on sustainable transportation,” CREA cofounder and report author Lauri Myllyvirta told Fortune . “Undoing that, of course, takes quite a bit of time and effort.”
The U.S. is heavily exposed to higher fuel costs in part because it is beholden to global market rates, a result of it still having to trade for heavy oil despite being a major diesel producer. But the heavier energy burden on American consumers is mostly because of the country’s reliance on oil over other sustainable means of energy, CREA argued.
The U.S. has less electric-vehicle adoption than other countries. And less efficient gas-powered cars travel farther on American roads compared to other countries, meaning American consumers simply burn more fuel than consumers in other countries, the report said. CREA found a positive correlation between countries with the greatest EV market share—Norway, Sweden, Finland, the Netherlands, and Belgium—and fuel cost savings per person.
Across the world, EV sales have surged as fuel costs have increased. In Denmark, for example, EVs made up 81% of new-vehicle sales in the first eight months of 2026. Nearly all new-vehicle sales in Norway over the same period were EVs, and 57% of new-vehicle sales in China were all-electric. Some European countries such as Germany saw a decrease in gas and diesel demand in 2026.
By comparison, only 7.3% of new-vehicle sales in the U.S. over that span were plug-in EVs, and the report found that American drivers who made the switch to eclectic cars saw only a $17 increase in charging costs since early March as a result of electricity price increases.
Myllyvirta suggested this pattern is primed to continue. A series of U.S. policy changes has disincentivized Americans from purchasing EVs and automakers from building fuel efficient vehicles.
The Trump administration ended a $7,500 tax credit on new EVs in September 2025 it claimed would devastate the auto industry. Analysts have cited the end of the incentive as the reason EV demand flattened in the U.S., and the reason why companies like Ford rolled back production on all-electric cars in favor of hybrid vehicles.
Last month, Trump released new fuel economy standards , loosening Biden-era regulatory requirements for fuel efficiency to mitigate pollution—a move the president said would make cars more affordable, but that environmentalists argued would drive up fuel costs and cancel out any vehicle savings.
According to Myllyvirta, increased fuel costs for Americans are poised to continue, even if the war ends. While energy prices will level out once this conflict is over, the reliance on gas-powered cars will mean a repetition of this cycle during the next energy shock.
“The only certainty is volatility,” he said. “Prices are going to come down, and then there are going to be new shocks. And as long as the reliance on oil continues, that cycle is going to play out with effects on consumers, with effects on inflation and economic policy.”
Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune , covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: 8-month Iran war looms over Israeli election as Egypt wades into Saudi's fight with the Houthis
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: 8-month Iran war looms over Israeli election as Egypt wades into Saudi's fight with the Houthis
articles.content_orig:
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.
While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.
International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran during a U.N. Security Council meeting on Tuesday to grant immediate access to his agency so it can verify the Islamic republic's nuclear materials.
The IAEA has not had access to key nuclear facilities in Iran since Israel and the United States launched strikes on nuclear sites in June 2025.
Nuclear facilities have also been hit in the latest war, and the IAEA has repeatedly called for access.
"I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions and to give the IAEA the information and access the agency requires, so that it can verify all relevant facilities and material, as is Iran's legal obligation," Grossi said.
The Security Council meeting followed a resolution passed by the IAEA board last month that referred Iran to the top U.N. body over its nuclear "non-compliance."
The resolution, submitted by Britain, France, Germany and the United States, marks the first time Iran has been referred to the Security Council in 20 years for failing to comply with its nuclear reporting obligations.
The move has been seen as largely symbolic as China and Russia hold power to veto any sanctions against their ally Tehran. Both countries were joined by Niger in voting against the IAEA resolution.
Nearly 100 fighters have been killed in renewed clashes between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces in southwestern Yemen, military sources from both sides told the AFP news agency on Tuesday.
At least 63 Houthi fighters and 34 pro-government combatants have died, mostly near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea's strategic southern chokepoint, they said.
The clashes, which began with airstrikes late on Monday, are the fiercest since the Houthis seized swathes of territory from the Saudi-backed government in a lightning offensive last month.
The Houthis fought off "an attempted advance by Saudi enemy forces ... from the southern direction of Bab al-Mandab," military spokesman Yahya Saree posted on X, describing "a large number of dead and wounded."
The Houthi military sources said Saudi Arabia carried out dozens of airstrikes, hitting Mayyun Island in the strait as well as Dhubab and Mocha further up the Red Sea coast.
Government military sources said intense fighting was under way in the Bab el-Mandeb area, claiming they had made progress on the ground.
Earlier this month, Yemen's government launched a counteroffensive with Saudi air support to try to reclaim the territory lost to the Houthis.
But the campaign has faltered, while the Houthis have ramped up deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia that shuttered its capital's airport for two weeks and disrupted daily life.
Riyadh leads a military coalition that first intervened in the conflict in 2015. The fighting has devastated Yemen and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, discussed working together on oil and gas projects as the two met in person at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum Summit in Moscow on Tuesday.
The two leaders "discussed expanding political, economic, trade and energy cooperation, including joint projects in the oil and gas sectors," according to a readout from the Iranian government .
Pezeshkian also discussed working together on natural gas exports. Iran ranks third in the world in natural gas production — 280 billion cubic meters per year, according to the president — behind only the U.S. and Russia.
"Pezeshkian emphasized that global developments necessitate joint technical-engineering cooperation and strategic governance across international energy markets," the government said, presumably referring to the war with the U.S.
Russia and Iran have worked together for years. As the war in Ukraine continues, Russia continues to purchase Shahed drones for use in attacks.
The two countries have rarely coordinated on energy projects, however, as both countries produce massive amounts of crude on their own. The timing of the discussion Tuesday in Russia is especially important though because Iran has been cut off from importing or exporting crude due to the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports.
France's deputy chief of mission in Tehran was this month subjected to "intimidation by individuals claiming to belong to the Iranian security forces," a diplomatic source told the AFP news agency on Tuesday.
The incident, the second involving French diplomats in Tehran in less than four months, highlights the sharp deterioration in relations between France and Iran.
In response to the mistreatment of the diplomat in early October, Iran's ambassador to France was summoned by the French foreign ministry, the source said, without specifying the exact date of the summons.
"He was reminded in the strongest terms that we expect the Iranian authorities to take all necessary measures to guarantee the security of our personnel and premises," the source said.
French magazine Le Point , which first reported the incident, said the diplomat was forcibly stopped in the street by members of Iran's security forces, in breach of his diplomatic status. The encounter culminated in what the magazine described as a forceful interrogation.
The episode follows a July incident involving two French diplomats based in Tehran.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot accused the Iranian authorities at the time of having "detained them without reason for several hours," adding one of them had been "physically manhandled."
Iran said at the time the diplomats had been "briefly questioned" by security services after attending a "meeting with several individuals wanted by the authorities," and denounced French "interference … under the pretext of engaging with civil society."
The Iran-backed Houthis claimed Thursday that they struck three different airports in southwestern Saudi Arabia, and repelled an advance by Saudi-affiliated forces from the southern direction of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on X that the group's forces had "succeeded in targeting two military transport aircraft with two ballistic missiles: the first at Najran Airport and the second at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait," both of which are in southwestern Saudi Arabia.
"Both operations successfully achieved their objectives, by the grace of God," he added.
In a separate statement on X , Saree said Houthi forces earlier thwarted an attempted advance by what he described as Saudi enemy forces "from the southern direction of Bab al-Mandab," the gateway to the Red Sea.

iOS 27.2 arrived this week with new features for Messages , Apple TV , and more, plus two improvements for CarPlay. Here’s what’s new for CarPlay users.
Apple Podcasts in iOS 27.2 adds two new sections to the Home tab: ‘New Episodes’ and ‘Continue Playing.’
Essentially, Apple has rethought how the core ‘Up Next’ queue of its Podcasts app works.
Like you would expect, ‘New Episodes’ contains only the latest episodes from your favorite shows. But after you’ve started an episode, you’ll find it in the ‘Continue Playing’ row just below.
This overhaul to podcast management makes it easier to find the latest episodes of your shows and also pick up where you previously left off. I’m a big fan of the change.
Siri AI introduces a variety of upgrades in iOS 27.2, including two that carry over to CarPlay as well.
Per Apple’s release notes :
It can take some adjustment to remember that Siri AI is available in the car just like on iPhone. But CarPlay is an especially useful platform for Apple’s more powerful assistant.
It’s arguable whether this qualifies as an “improvement,” but it is a change worth mentioning. iOS 27.2 includes a new app icon for Apple Music, plus some minor design tweaks in the app.
These changes are related to the total rebrand Apple Music unveiled just last week.

articles.title_orig: Why Is Halloween Candy So Expensive?
articles.title_zh: Why Is Halloween Candy So Expensive?
articles.content_orig:
Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.
If you can’t afford a trip to a haunted house this spooky season, just swing by the supermarket candy aisle for a nasty scare. The price of sweets jumped over the last few years, soaring even faster than the average inflation rate, according to a recent report from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, with higher ingredient costs as the primary villain.
October is important for candy sales, as shoppers stock up for parties, trick-or-treaters, or — let’s be honest — personal consumption.
“The biggest purchasing days are still ahead, with about 35% of Halloween seasonal sales expected this week,” a Hershey Company spokesperson told CNET.
Chocolate treats have become especially expensive, as a recent global cocoa shortage squeezed the market while candy companies were preparing shipments for Halloween.
But despite chilling prices, chocolate is still making its way into Halloween bags and buckets.
“Trick-or-treat participation intent is in line with last year,” the Hershey spokesperson said. “Confection remains a resilient category.”
Americans will likely spend over $13 billion on Halloween this year, the National Retail Federation reports . That’s almost twice the $6.9 billion people spent on the holiday 11 years ago, in 2015.
“Consumers continue to make Halloween a spending priority, but they are also approaching the season with affordability in mind,” Allison Zeller, a National Retail Federation vice president, said in a statement.
Candy remains the favorite purchase, with 95% of Halloween shoppers planning to snag some this year, followed by decorations, costumes and greeting cards, according to the National Retail Federation. In 2026, shoppers are expected to spend over $4 billion on Halloween candy alone.
An Oct. 20 report from research group Groundwork Collaborative broke down which candy prices have risen the most this year. The Mondelez Sour Gummy Candy variety pack, which jumped 39% in price, and Hershey seasonal Peanut Butter Cups, which saw a 23% increase, are this year’s most expensive Halloween candy compared with last season.
The squeeze doesn’t stop in the candy aisle — utility bills and other essentials are climbing, too. A Consumer Reports survey from earlier this month found that one in five American families has cut back on groceries due to rising energy costs.
“If you’ve been waiting until now to get your Halloween goodies, you’re right to do so. Halloween sales hit the high street and online two or three days before Halloween as stores try to clear stock,” says James Bricknell, CNET commerce managing editor.
“If you’re all set for this year, do what I did last year and grab a bunch of costumes and decorations the day after Halloween,” he adds. “Then, you can store them ready to go for Halloween 2027.”

articles.title_orig: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
articles.title_zh: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
articles.content_orig:
Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools.
The memo , which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI.
"We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice."
Under CEO Andy Jassy , Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations. Jassy has previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs."
As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology's surging costs and how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment.
Companies have recently cracked down on tokenmaxxing , in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks.
An Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks.
In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity.
It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said.
"We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote.
Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity.
The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said.
"Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those."
He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation."
Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task.
"If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo.
The company added, "An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for."

articles.title_orig: Hasbro Appoints Dungeons & Dragons VP As Next President Of Wizards Of The Coast
articles.title_zh: Hasbro Appoints Dungeons & Dragons VP As Next President Of Wizards Of The Coast
articles.content_orig:
Hasbro has named Dan Ayoub the next President of Wizards of the Coast (WotC) & Hasbro Digital Games.
Announced in a press release from Hasbro earlier today, Ayoub was reportedly selected from a sizeable pool of “…internal and external candidates…” after an extensive three-month search, and is the “…first internal candidate” to be promoted to the role of President.
A seasoned veteran of the industry, Ayoub’s background includes 25 years of experience making video games, headlined by over a decade with Microsoft and Halo studio 343 Industries. Ayoub joined WotC back in 2022 initially as Senior Vice President of Digital Games, but most recently served as Senior Vice President of Dungeons & Dragons.
According to Hasbro CEO, Chris Cocks, who has been acting as WotC’s interim President since John Hight relinquished the role back in September , Ayoub “…has the passion and leadership caliber to take Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro Digital Games into its next chapter…” and is “…excited for the future with him at the helm.”
As President of WotC, Ayoub will oversee the Magic: The Gathering, Dungeons & Dragons, and Duel Masters brands, as well as Hasbro’s digital games segment.
“I’m honored to lead Wizards of the Coast and Hasbro Digital Games, and grateful to Chris and the leadership team for this opportunity. Magic and D&D have been part of my life for as long as I can remember, and the teams behind them are among the best in the world. We’ll put fans first, respect the artists and creators who make these worlds come alive, and set an ambitious course for growth across tabletop and digital. I can’t wait to get started.”
Per today’s news release, Ayoub is expected to start his new role on Monday, November 2.

articles.title_orig: Trump allies fall in two elections as Netanyahu faces next test
articles.title_zh: Trump allies fall in two elections as Netanyahu faces next test
articles.content_orig:
When news breaks, you need to understand what actually matters — and what to do about it. At Vox, our mission to help you make sense of the world has never been more vital. But we can’t do it on our own.
We rely on readers like you to fund our journalism. Will you support our work and become a Vox Member today?
In Serbia and Brazil, huge numbers of voters turned out on Sunday to repudiate right-wing populists.
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .
Vox isn’t typically in the business of covering elections in far-flung locales like the central Balkans. (No offense whatsoever to anyone from the central Balkans!) But on Sunday, an insurgent student-backed movement in Serbia successfully toppled the country’s ruling right-wing political machine, creating an unexpected opening for democratic reform.
Then, in another upset halfway around the globe, Brazilian voters reelected incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva over his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro. “Democracy always, dictatorship never again,” Lula said in his victory speech.
That’s two big repudiations of the nationalist right in 24 hours. Not quite enough to declare a trend, maybe, but sufficient to remind us that there’s still hope for the world’s embattled democratic institutions.
More than that, these results offer evidence of something that sounds naive and Pollyannish in our current moment, but can (apparently!) still prove true: Organizing can be a powerful force for electoral change — both abroad and maybe here at home.
To be fair, the two elections differed considerably, and I don’t want to suggest it’s all sunshine and democratic renewal ahead for Brazil and Serbia. Bolsonaro is refusing to concede, for instance. And in Serbia, the victorious Student List still has to stand up a government, a prime minister, and a full policy platform — something the nascent movement has never done before.
But academics and elections-watchers in both countries have credited the results in large part to mass protests and grassroots organizing that helped mobilize unexpected numbers of voters .
Serbian students began their movement in 2024, following the partial collapse of a railway station that killed 16 people. The government’s failure to fully explain the cause of the collapse — or hold anyone responsible — fueled months of marches, protest bike rides, and other demonstrations. That movement eventually grew into the Student List: an opposition electoral slate that fielded 250 candidates in Sunday’s parliamentary elections.
The story in Brazil is quite different. Lula, the country’s leftist president, was actually poised to lose. Brazil uses a two-round popular vote to elect its president, and if no candidate secures more than half the vote in the first round, then the top two candidates proceed to a runoff election. Lula placed second in that first vote, after Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and the heir to his father’s far-right political movement.
To many Brazilians, that second-place finish served as a kind of wake-up call. “No runoff campaign in Brazil has ever brought so many people to the streets and onto social media,” Guilherme Casarões , an associate professor of Brazilian studies at Florida International University, wrote in an analysis of the surprise results. One WhatsApp channel dedicated to turning voters out for Lula grew to nearly 11 million followers , up from just 50,000 after his first-round loss.
Looking at these projects abroad, I’m struck that American pro-democracy movements like No Kings haven’t achieved that kind of influence. Arguably, that’s in part a consequence of their failure to turn protest energy into actual political organizing — things like registering voters, knocking on doors, and fielding candidates.
But there are some signs that may be shifting. No Kings has lately pivoted its focus, for instance, from mostly organizing protests to urging Americans — of both parties — to vote in the midterms. And Indivisible, one of the groups behind the movement, claims that early voting surged during the latest protests in the zip codes where they occurred.
It’s not exactly a central Balkan moment, but maybe it’s a hint of things to come. Elections can surprise you, after all. Just ask a Serb or a Brazilian.
➨ Leave your big life decisions to chance. (Sort of.) A team of researchers invited people to make a big life decision by flipping a coin and then tracked their happiness with the outcome. They found that, of the people who obeyed the results of the toss, the ones who changed something big were overwhelmingly happier. That doesn’t literally mean we should all resort to coin tosses, but it should tell us something important: We often tend to be too cautious about making major changes .

articles.title_orig: Amid the Anthropic IPO excitement, don't forget about earnings season
articles.title_zh: Amid the Anthropic IPO excitement, don't forget about earnings season
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
We are only two days into the week, and it already feels like it should be the weekend.
In the past two days, Meta ( META ) said it will raise $95 billion to support its AI build-out through stock offerings, and Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) dropped a 407-page IPO prospectus that I know you haven't read in its entirety. (Wall Street hasn't either, so don't lose sleep over it.)
Lost in that activity is that earnings season continues in full swing, with results from Coca-Cola ( KO ), Hilton ( HLT ), UPS ( UPS ), Whirlpool ( WHR ), and others today.
While investors are jacked up about AI and some stability returning to the tech trade, don't lose sight of earnings season: After all, it's earnings and earnings expectations that power stocks, not Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei (although his comments have moved markets in the past).
So here are a few quick takes on a couple of earnings reports I chewed through this morning:
I don't have any problems with this Hilton quarter, even though the stock is getting hit on a slight revenue miss. The important revenue per available room metric grew 5.8%, the company remains an aggressive buyer of its stock, and it approved the development of 30,500 rooms in the quarter.
The report fits nicely with the Delta ( DAL ) report we got last week, in that higher fuel prices don't appear to be slowing leisure or business travelers.
I think it also fits nicely with the numbers out of UPS today, with US sales up 4.5% and its full-year guidance hike.
Coca-Cola's latest guidance lift reinforces the view that the company continues to take massive market share away from rival PepsiCo ( PEP ). Coke Zero sales surged 16%.
Not a good day for the team at PepsiCo up in Purchase, N.Y.
I continue to be absolutely shocked by what's happening at Whirlpool ( WHR ). Another supersoft quarter, with an adjusted loss of $0.21 per share. Costs are up, and the business is being hurt by a near-frozen US housing market.
You need nerves of steel to buy Whirlpool shares here — the stock is down more than 63% this year. If you do, the thesis has to be that the iconic company is acquired at some point in the next 12 months.

The partner set to take over leadership of Weil, Gotshal & Manges has held talks to leave the firm for a rival, a move that would compound ongoing talent drain at one of Wall Streetâs top dealmaking and restructuring shops.
Ramona Nee, Weilâs co-managing partner, has had discussions to join Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, according to people familiar with the matter. Nee, an adviser to big private equity firms including Advent, was slated to take over as Weilâs sole chair in January.
Weil declined to comment. Nee did not return a request for comment. Her departure is not guaranteed and the talks could fall apart, the people said.
If she does leave, she would follow a flood of Weilâs top talent out the door and the breakdown of merger talks with crosstown rival Willkie Farr & Gallagher. Rainmaker Michael Aiello defected to Cravath, Swaine & Moore with a team of partners. It would be likely that a sizable portion of Weilâs Boston partnership would leave with her, according to one person familiar with the matter who is close with many of Weilâs top Boston lawyers.
Nee had told Weil partners she would not take the chair job, which was announced last spring, according to a person briefed on the communication. The Financial Times earlier reported that decision.
Remaining and former Weil lawyers place blame on Aielloâs departure â and Neeâs possible departure â at the feet of executive partner Barry Wolf, who has helmed the firm to some success for more than a decade but in recent years has failed to convince senior partners that Weil has a vision for a world where AI and outsize pay packages upend the perceived usefulness of high-end legal advice.
Aielloâs departure came as a result, in part, because top Weil leaders including Wolf failed to lay out a convincing long-term vision for the firm, according to a person familiar with his thinking.

articles.title_orig: The secret succession rankings that Anthropic shareholders will never see (unless the company is ordered)
articles.title_zh: The secret succession rankings that Anthropic shareholders will never see (unless the company is ordered)
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic has devised an unusual way for its founders to pass on their power.
In its IPO filings , Anthropic outlined how seven of its cofounders, who collectively have 50.1% of voting control, will be able to create a ranked list of who they'd like to inherit their power in the event of their death or incapacitation.
What's particularly notable is that while the names would be shared with the other LLC members and Anthropic's Nominating Committee, they are otherwise contractually confidential and generally not public.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , Anthropic President Daniela Amodei, and the five other LLC members will review and vote on whether to approve their fellow founders' proposed successors, but the names will likely never be seen by other shareholders. (The agreement allows for the publication only in narrow circumstances, such as a court order or other legal requirement.)
Under the agreement, which was first highlighted by Forbes , each member of the Founders LLC may name up to 10 potential successors, ranked in order of preference. The other LLC members must then vote to approve the secret lists.
While succession plans are not unusual, Anthropic's approach is unusual in how it ranks potential successors. It also underscores how, thanks to the Founders LLC, Anthropic's leaders will be able to maintain control as shareholders begin to offer input post-IPO.
Facebook's 2012 IPO paperwork suggested that if Mark Zuckerberg were in control of the company at the time of his death, then control could be transferred to someone he designated. (Meta has since tweaked this plan.) In 2020, Airbnb's three cofounders agreed to transfer their voting power to their other cofounders if one of them died or became disabled, but that arrangement (which still exists) only lasts for nine months.
The succession plan does not establish CEO succession. Anthropic's board of directors would handle such a chief executive appointment.
There are also some limitations to who the Anthropic founders can name on their lists.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Eight of their 10 potential successors are subject to eligibility requirements, including that the person named is a current or former employee of Anthropic or one of its subsidiaries, or has worked for "a 501(c)(3) tax-exempt organization or a national or international organization whose primary purpose is research, education, or the promotion of public benefit." In either case, the person must have worked there for at least three years.
If the person worked for Anthropic, they must have held a specific role, such as a member of the technical staff or the company's internal think tank, or another role approved by the board and a majority of the other members. If they worked outside Anthropic, they must have held a senior role at the nonprofit. These successors must also be US citizens, have permanent residency, or have valid work authorization.
The other two names, if a founder names all 10 potential successors, are not subject to the eligibility requirements, but they must also receive the required approval.
The succession plan doesn't last forever.
Under the agreement, a successor member generally would cease to be a member on the 10th anniversary of Anthropic's IPO. After that point, successor designees may be admitted only in limited circumstances during a transition period.

articles.title_orig: Fed meeting live updates: Federal Reserve weighs elevated inflation, midterm elections as October meeting kicks off
articles.title_zh: Fed meeting live updates: Federal Reserve weighs elevated inflation, midterm elections as October meeting kicks off
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The Federal Reserve kicked off its two-day policy meeting on Tuesday as elevated inflation continues to pose a problem for central bankers who nevertheless seem reluctant to hike rates this month.
Fed watchers expect the central bank to keep benchmark rates in the 3.75% to 4% range , with bond traders pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike on Wednesday, per CME Group. A rate hike in December appears far more likely, however, according to the Fed's dot plot and fed funds futures.
Although recent inflation data came in hotter than expected , several officials' remarks suggest the Fed will hold rates this month to continue assessing additional data. The proximity of the October meeting to the US midterm elections next Tuesday is also seen as a deterrent to bold monetary policy moves.
With the Fed holding rates steady seen as all but given, the focus is on what Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will say at his post-FOMC-meeting press conference on Wednesday. Warsh has deliberately avoided telegraphing future Fed policy moves, but hot inflation could elicit more insight from him into the path forward.
Markets are heading into a busy few days for global central bank rate announcements.
Five major central banks are scheduled to make policy decisions this week, with two expected to hike and three to hold.
On Wednesday, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Bank of Canada will announce their decisions before the Fed releases its FOMC statement. Both central banks are expected to hike rates.
In Canada's case, the BOC is caught between a weakening economy and higher inflation. Governor Tiff Macklem has signaled in recent months that he is concerned about higher oil prices bleeding through to broader price inflation.
The next day, the European Central Bank is expected to hold rates steady, as is the Bank of Japan on Friday.
Many economists see the overall bias of central banks tilting toward tighter policy next year as artificial intelligence and the war in the Middle East drive inflation higher.
"If you're a central banker ... you've got to recognize this as a shock," Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said about AI at the IMF annual meeting this month.
The major US stock indexes rose on Tuesday as investors anticipated the Fed's decision on Wednesday.
The Dow ( ^DJI ) edged just above the flat line, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) rose 0.6% and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) gained 1.2% amid a semiconductor stock rally.
The US dollar index ( DX-Y.NYB ) rose above 102, and the 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) remained steady at 4.99%. Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) also rose to above $80,600.
Conviction that the Fed would hold rates steady firmed on Tuesday, with traders expecting just 7% odds of a hike. Unless the Fed opts for a surprise hike, the decision is unlikely to move markets much.
But watch what happens to assets when Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh begins speaking tomorrow. Investors will be on alert for any hawkish signals.
The Federal Open Market Committee's two-day policy meeting has started and will conclude at 2 p.m. ET on Wednesday.
The FOMC's decision on whether to cut, hold, or raise interest rates will be released at 2 p.m. tomorrow. Following that decision, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh will hold a news conference at 2:30 p.m. that will be live-streamed.
This is the seventh FOMC meeting this year. The final Fed meeting of the year will take place from Dec. 8-9 and will include a Summary of Economic Projections, which will be used to gauge where policymakers see rates heading in 2027.
The Federal Reserve heads into its interest-rate decision this week facing hotter inflation, keeping the meeting live even as markets widely expect the central bank to hold interest rates steady just days before the midterm elections.
Alan Blinder, a former Fed vice chair and a Princeton University economics professor, is expecting a "hawkish pause."
Although Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh doesn't favor telegraphing the central bank's next move, Blinder said the moment calls for clarity.
"This is a perfect time for clear forward guidance that doesn't quite say, but strongly hints, we're pausing now, but we stand ready to raise again and even give a hint that the next meeting might be the next interest rate hike."
The Federal Reserve's two-day policy meeting kicked off this morning at 9:30 a.m. ET, as scheduled, a Fed spokesperson confirmed.
Expectations remain firm that the Fed will hold rates steady in a range of 3.75% to 4% after hiking by 25 basis points in September. Traders broadly view that the Fed will hike again in December.
But in October, there's a strong belief the Fed won't move rates. According to CME Group's FedWatch, traders see a 90% chance of no move.
